docs.title: How to Use This Outline
docs.text:
Three layers, so start wherever fits the moment:

  • Preface — a single fast read: the whole process compressed into a few pages, meant to cut the "where do I even start" panic and hand over five concrete first steps.
  • Parts One through Five — the comprehensive guide, one deep-dive chapter per topic, written so any chapter stands alone when that topic becomes urgent.
  • Appendix — a month-by-month planner that turns the whole book into a checklist tied to the real senior-year calendar.

Written to the student, but just as useful read alongside a parent or counselor.

docs.title: Preface — The Quick-Start Synopsis
docs.text:
(5–8 pages)

  • The process in one page — a simplified timeline: build your list → test → apply → seek aid → decide → enroll, running from senior fall through the following fall.
  • Five things to do this week — a short starter checklist: set up a shared tracker, create your Common App / Coalition account, ask two teachers for recommendations, draft an activities resume, start a running list of essay material.
  • Three myths, debunked — there's no single "right" school; test-optional doesn't mean tests never matter; admissions isn't just about being well-rounded.
  • A note on stress — normalizing uncertainty, reframing rejection as fit rather than failure, and setting the expectation that this takes months, not days.

docs.title: Part One: Laying the Groundwork
docs.text:
Chapters 1–3

  1. Understanding How Admissions Works — holistic review explained; what colleges actually weigh; reach/target/safety; public vs. private; early decision vs. early action vs. regular decision.
  2. Building Your College List — a self-assessment (fit, cost, size, location, majors); research tools and how to use them; narrowing a long list to 8–12 schools.
  3. Getting Organized — deadline trackers, accounts to set up (Common App, Coalition, individual portals), and a simple filing system for transcripts, essays, and login info.

docs.title: Part Two: Testing & Academics
docs.text:
Chapters 4–5

  1. The SAT/ACT Question — the test-optional landscape and how to decide whether to submit scores; prep strategies that don't require a $2,000 tutor; superscoring and when to retest.
  2. Your Senior Year Course Load — why senior grades still matter after you've applied; choosing AP, IB, or dual enrollment; balancing rigor against burnout.

docs.title: Part Three: Building the Application
docs.text:
Chapters 6–11

  1. Activities & Resume — presenting extracurriculars, jobs, and family responsibilities as strengths; showing depth over a long list.
  2. The Personal Essay — brainstorming techniques, working the Common App prompts, drafting and revising for voice and authenticity.
  3. Supplemental Essays — "Why us" essays, short-answer questions, and avoiding the recycled-essay trap.
  4. Letters of Recommendation — who to ask, how to ask, and what to give recommenders so they can write a strong letter.
  5. Filling Out the Common App / Coalition App — a line-by-line walkthrough of the sections that trip students up.
  6. Interviews — when they matter, how to prepare, and what colleges are actually listening for.

docs.title: Part Four: Paying for College
docs.text:
Chapters 12–14

  1. Understanding Financial Aid — FAFSA and CSS Profile basics; need-based vs. merit aid; what "net price" really means.
  2. Scholarships — where to actually find them, how to prioritize applications, and avoiding scholarship scams.
  3. Comparing Award Letters — reading an aid offer line by line; loans vs. grants; requesting a reconsideration.

docs.title: Part Five: Decisions & the Finish Line
docs.text:
Chapters 15–18

  1. Waiting & Managing Anxiety — what actually happens to an application after submission, and how to stay sane during the wait.
  2. Handling Decisions — accept, deny, and waitlist strategies; appealing a financial aid offer.
  3. Making Your Final Choice — comparing offers side by side, revisiting campuses, and committing by May 1.
  4. Getting Ready for Fall — housing forms, orientation, AP credit, and the gap between high school graduation and move-in day.

docs.title: Appendix: Month-by-Month Senior Year Planner
docs.text:
• August–September — Finalize your college list. Start the Common App. Request transcripts. Begin brainstorming your essay.
  • October — Take or retake the SAT/ACT. Draft essays. Request letters of recommendation. Submit Early Action/Early Decision applications.
  • November — Finish supplemental essays. Submit regular-decision applications with early deadlines. FAFSA opens — file it.
  • December — Continue regular-decision applications. Confirm recommenders have submitted. Watch for mid-year grade requests.
  • January — Submit remaining regular-decision applications. Meet CSS Profile deadlines. Apply for outside scholarships.
  • February — Finish scholarship applications. Respond promptly to any financial aid follow-up requests.
  • March — Decisions start arriving. Begin comparing offers as they come in.
  • April — Compare final financial aid packages. Visit or revisit top schools. Decide before May 1.
  • May — Send your deposit. Decline other offers. Take AP exams. Send your final transcript to your chosen school.
  • June–August — Complete housing forms, orientation, and health requirements. Connect with your roommate. Prepare for move-in.

docs.title: Course Overview
docs.text:
Title: College Admissions Roadmap

Target Audience: High school students, mainly rising seniors and seniors, who are applying to four-year colleges in the United States. The book speaks to the student directly, and parents, guardians, and school counselors can use it alongside the student.

Prerequisites: None. You don't need any prior knowledge of the admissions process, financial aid, or college application platforms. It helps to have your own high school transcript, activity history, and a rough idea of your family's finances on hand.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text: Applying to college is one of the first big, high-stakes projects a student manages mostly on their own. It has dozens of deadlines, several online platforms, and financial decisions that can shape the next decade. Much of the process isn't written down, so students with a private counselor or a college-educated parent start ahead. This book lays out the whole roadmap: what colleges actually weigh, how to present yourself honestly and well, how to pay for college, and how to choose. The goal is that any student can run the process with confidence instead of panic.

docs.title: Main Topics Covered
docs.text:
1. How admissions works: holistic review, what colleges weigh, reach/target/safety schools, public vs. private, and Early Decision vs. Early Action vs. Regular Decision.
  2. Building and organizing a college list: self-assessment for fit, research tools, narrowing to 8–12 schools, and deadline trackers, accounts, and filing systems.
  3. Testing and academics: the test-optional landscape, deciding whether to submit scores, low-cost test prep, superscoring, and senior-year course rigor (AP, IB, dual enrollment).
  4. Activities and the resume: presenting extracurriculars, jobs, and family responsibilities, with depth over breadth.
  5. Essays: the Common App personal essay, supplemental "Why us" and short-answer essays, brainstorming, drafting, and revision.
  6. Recommendations, the application platforms, and interviews: choosing and supporting recommenders, walking through the Common App / Coalition App, and interview preparation.
  7. Paying for college: the FAFSA and CSS Profile, need-based vs. merit aid, net price, scholarships and scholarship scams, and reading and comparing award letters.
  8. Decisions and enrollment: managing the wait, handling admits, denials, and waitlists, appealing aid offers, committing by May 1, and preparing for fall (housing, orientation, AP credit).
  9. Month-by-month senior-year planning: turning the process into a calendar-based checklist.

docs.title: Topics Not Covered
docs.text:
• Graduate, professional, law, or medical school admissions
  • Transfer admissions from a community college or another four-year school
  • International student admissions, visas, and non-U.S. application systems (e.g., UCAS)
  • Athletic recruiting and NCAA eligibility rules in detail
  • Arts portfolio and audition requirements in depth
  • Detailed subject-by-subject SAT/ACT content review
  • Choosing a career or major in depth
  • Personal financial planning beyond paying for college (e.g., 529 plan investment strategy)

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text: After this course, students will be able to:

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
• List the main stages of the admissions process in order: build the list, test, apply, seek aid, decide, enroll.
  • Recall the key senior-year deadlines, including Early Action/Early Decision dates, the FAFSA opening date, CSS Profile deadlines, and the May 1 commitment date.
  • Name the major application platforms (Common App, Coalition App, institutional portals) and the financial aid forms (FAFSA, CSS Profile).
  • Identify the parts of an application: transcript, test scores, activities list, personal essay, supplemental essays, recommendations, and interview.
  • Define key terms such as holistic review, superscoring, net price, need-based aid, merit aid, and waitlist.

docs.title: Understand
docs.text:
• Explain how holistic review weighs grades, rigor, essays, activities, and recommendations together.
  • Describe the differences among Early Decision, Early Action, Restrictive Early Action, and Regular Decision, including whether each is binding.
  • Explain what "test-optional" means in practice and why test scores can still matter.
  • Distinguish grants, scholarships, work-study, and loans, and explain why net price matters more than sticker price.
  • Explain why senior-year grades still count after applications are submitted.
  • Summarize what happens to an application after it is submitted.

docs.title: Apply
docs.text:
• Use a self-assessment and research tools to build a college list of 8–12 schools.
  • Set up a deadline tracker, the required accounts, and a filing system for transcripts, essays, and logins.
  • Complete the sections of the Common App or Coalition App accurately.
  • File the FAFSA (and CSS Profile where required) on time.
  • Follow the month-by-month planner to schedule tasks across senior year.
  • Prepare a recommender packet and make a clear, timely request to teachers and counselors.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text:
• Sort schools on a list into reach, target, and safety using admission data and your own academic profile.
  • Break down an award letter line by line to separate free money from loans and find the true out-of-pocket cost.
  • Compare your test scores with a school's middle-50% range to decide whether submitting them helps or hurts.
  • Examine your activities and experiences to find themes and depth worth highlighting.
  • Analyze a school's mission, programs, and culture to find specific, genuine points for a "Why us" essay.

docs.title: Evaluate
docs.text:
• Judge whether to submit test scores to each school on your list.
  • Decide whether Early Decision is financially and personally wise for your top choice.
  • Weigh competing admission offers by fit, net cost, debt load, and outcomes to make a final choice.
  • Assess scholarship opportunities for legitimacy, spot scams, and prioritize applications by expected value.
  • Critique and revise your own essay drafts for voice, authenticity, and focus.
  • Judge whether and how to appeal a financial aid offer or respond to a waitlist.

docs.title: Create
docs.text:
• Write a personal Common App essay and a set of supplemental essays in your own voice.
  • Build an activities resume that presents extracurriculars, jobs, and family responsibilities as strengths.
  • Create a personalized month-by-month senior-year plan with every application, test, and financial aid deadline.
  • Draft a financial aid appeal or reconsideration letter backed by specific evidence.
  • Capstone: Build a complete application roadmap for one real school of your choice, covering the school's platform and testing policy, your essay plan, recommendation requests, aid and scholarship timeline, a projected net price, and enrollment steps.

docs.title: Learning Graph for College Admissions Roadmap
docs.text:
Open Learning Graph Viewer Fullscreen

This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Course Description Quality Assessment
docs.text:
This report rates the overall quality of the course description for the purpose of generating a learning graph.

  • Course description fields and content depth analysis
  • Validates course description has sufficient depth for generating 300-600 concepts
  • Compares course description against similar courses
  • Identifies content gaps and strengths
  • Suggests areas of improvement View the Course Description Quality Assessment

docs.title: Learning Graph Quality Validation
docs.text:
This report gives you an overall assessment of the quality of the learning graph. It uses graph algorithms to look for specific quality patterns in the graph.

  • Graph structure validation - all concepts are connected
  • DAG validation (no cycles detected)
  • Foundational concepts: 5 entry points
  • Indegree distribution analysis
  • Longest dependency chains
  • Connectivity: percent of nodes connected to the main cluster

View the Learning Graph Quality Validation

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
In order to see patterns in the learning graph, it is useful to assign colors to each concept based on the concept type. We use generative AI to create about a dozen categories for our concepts and then place each concept into a single primary classifier.

  • A concept classifier taxonomy with approximately 12 categories (+/- 1 or 2)
  • Category organization - foundational elements first, course capstone project ideas last
  • Balanced categories (3.5% - 15% each)
  • All categories under 30% threshold
  • Pedagogical flow recommendations
  • Clear 3-5 letter abbreviations for use in CSV file
  • A Miscellaneous (MISC) category is sometimes added View the Concept Taxonomy

docs.title: Taxonomy Distribution
docs.text:
This reports shows how many concepts fit into each category of the taxonomy. Our goal is a somewhat balanced taxonomy where each category holds an equal number of concepts. We also don't want any category to contain over 30% of our concepts.

  • Statistical breakdown
  • Detailed concept listing by category
  • Visual distribution table
  • Balance verification

View the Taxonomy Distribution Report

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text:
The 342 concepts in the College Admissions Roadmap learning graph are grouped into 13 categories. Each category has a short TaxonomyID used in learning-graph.csv and the graph viewer legend.

Category TaxonomyID Concepts What belongs here Admissions Foundations FOUND 39 How selective admissions works: holistic and formula-based review, GPA and course rigor, types of colleges, residency, application rounds (ED/EA/RD), and the common myths. College List Building LIST 31 Self-assessment, the dimensions of fit, reach/target/safety, research tools and data sources, campus visits, and narrowing to a final list. docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
1. Main Topics Covered (9/10): Topic 6 (recommendations, application platforms, interviews) and Topic 7 (all of paying for college) are broad. The detailed outline above them covers each chapter separately, so the learning-graph generator still has the detail it needs. Having them as separate topics would make taxonomy categories cleaner.
  2. Remember (9/10): "Recall the key senior-year deadlines" is right for students, but the specific dates change each admissions cycle (the FAFSA opening date has moved in recent years). Concepts built from this outcome should focus on the type of deadline and where to check it, not fixed dates.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions (optional)
docs.text:
1. Consider splitting Topic 7 into "Financial aid forms and aid types" and "Scholarships and award letters." That would make the financial topics their own taxonomy category.
  2. Consider adding a Remember outcome such as "Identify where to find each school's current deadlines and policies." That would anchor the date-sensitive concepts to a lasting skill.
  3. When the book's dates are updated for a new cycle, re-check the Appendix planner against the current FAFSA and CSS Profile calendars.

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
• Topic breadth: 9 topics across 5 parts, a preface, and an appendix. That's a wide surface covering process, testing, writing, finance, decisions, and planning.
  • Topic depth: Each of the 18 chapters names 3–6 subtopics (e.g., holistic review, superscoring, net price, CSS Profile, waitlist strategy).
  • Concept diversity: The outcomes span vocabulary (Remember), mechanisms (Understand), procedures (Apply), comparisons (Analyze), judgments (Evaluate), and products (Create). That mix produces foundational, intermediate, and terminal concepts.
  • Estimated concept yield: About 220–260 concepts, enough for a 200+ concept learning graph.
